transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-16 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Lacuna Head of ML), Omar Ruiz (Infra Lead), Priya Patel (PM)

Auto-summary: Quick sync on pilot economics; agree next benchmark run and doc handoffs.

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda — short run through the numbers we sent, dig into batching and caching wins, then next steps. Maya, do you want to start with any new context on traffic?
[00:20] Maya: Yeah, thanks. We pushed a small change last week so traffic shape shifted a bit more conversational — average prompt length up, so token output increased. Our key metric is cost per satisfied response, but tokens per dollar is easiest for the bench.
[00:35] Daniel: Great, that's important cause the longer outputs amplify KV cache reuse in some cases. From the run we did yesterday — which, quick note, used the Redwood Dedicata profile — we saw about a 22% reduction in billable tokens when prefix caching was enabled across the canonical prompts.
[00:56] Priya: Sorry can I just clarify, when you say 22% is that absolute tokens saved or effective cost savings?
[01:02] Daniel: Good point. It's raw tokens saved — so roughly 22% fewer tokens consumed on average per session. Effective cost savings were about 18% after accounting for slightly higher p95 due to batching.
[01:20] Omar: Wait, batching increased p95? I thought batching always helped latency.
[01:25] Daniel: It depends. With batch size at 8 we improved throughput ~1.9x but p95 latency went up by roughly 60–90ms depending on sequence length. For user-facing synchronous flows, that matters; for background async ranking it might be fine.
[01:46] Maya: That tradeoff is exactly our pain. We need sub-300ms p95 on the chat front. If batching pushes us over, the user metrics degrade.
[01:55] Ava: Right — that's the classic latency vs cost. Two levers: lower batch size for chat paths; route background jobs to a high-batch pool. We can route by policy. Also quantization: Daniel, what did we see on 4-bit run?
[02:12] Daniel: 4-bit quant reduced cost about 35% in token dollars on our test model, with a small quality delta — roughly 2–3% drop on our internal eval set, but result depends on prompt sensitivity. Worth testing with customer prompts.
[02:30] Priya: Any weird hallucination patterns after quant?
[02:32] Daniel: A few edge cases where numeric precision matters; not common for your templates but we'll validate.
[02:40] Maya: Can you break down the tokens/sec/$ metric? Your sheet had a column tokens per second per dollar which confused the team.
[02:47] Ava: Yeah, that metric is a bit overloaded, sorry. Think of two separate: throughput per dollar (tokens/sec per dollar of spend rate) and tokens per dollar (tokens per $1 consumed). The former captures instant throughput economics for scaling, the latter is overall cost efficiency. We can convert to tokens-per-request too.
[03:06] Omar: For our infra planning we need peak tokens/sec requirements under the expected concurrency. Can Redwood run a 2-hour stress test emulating 50 concurrent users and give tokens/sec curves and cost projection?
[03:18] Ava: Yes — Daniel will run that with and without KV/prefix caching, and with batch sizes 1, 4, and 8. We'll share the CSV.
[03:25] Daniel: Plan is to run: baseline (no cache, batch=1), cache-only (batch=1), batch variants (batch=4 and 8), and quantized model at batch=4. We'll report p50/p95/p99 latencies plus tokens consumed and computed tokens-per-dollar.
[03:40] Priya: Also we need to know how failover affects cost. If you fall back to hosted model because of capacity, does cost spike?
[03:47] Ava: There's a fallback policy — you can set priority to prefer dedicated or allow fallback to hosted. Fallback often incurs higher unit cost, yes, but availability improves. We can show historical scenarios from other pilots where fallback only triggered during short bursts.
[04:05] Maya: Security question — KMS integration for key management. We are HIPAA-adjacent, need to ensure keys never leave our control.
[04:12] Ava: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and you can deploy the control plane in your VPC. We'll send the network diagram and KMS integration notes.
[04:20] Omar: Also SSO and RBAC for the console — we only want a couple of engineers to access model tuning.
[04:25] Daniel: SSO via SAML/SCIM, and role-based access is configurable per project. We'll include the docs.
[04:33] Maya: Back to economics — what real numbers did you see in tokens per dollar? The sheet had 150k tokens per dollar for baseline but that felt optimistic.
[04:42] Daniel: Baseline for the medium-size open model we used was ~120k tokens per $1 with batch=1, cache off. With prefix caching and batch=4 we moved to ~185k tokens per $1. Quantized model bumped that to ~250k tokens per $1 in lab conditions. Again, your mix of prompt lengths will change that.
[05:05] Priya: So the authoritative test is our real prompt set, realistic concurrency.
[05:08] Ava: Exactly. Hence the agreed run. Also, note tokens per dollar can be misleading if latency SLOs are missed; a cheaper config that breaks p95 isn't acceptable.
[05:21] Omar: For VPC peering, do you need an open IP range? We have restricted egress.
[05:27] Ava: We can work with an IP allowlist and private peering. We'll document required ports and addresses.
[05:34] Daniel: One more note on KV cache — it's most beneficial when you have repeated prefixes. From your sample prompts it looked like 40% of sessions shared a common instruction prefix, that's why savings are higher. If your prefix diversity increases, the percent saved drops.
[05:49] Maya: Good to know. We'll attach distribution.
[05:52] Priya: Anything on A/B test support? We might want to run two rollout configs.
[05:56] Ava: Console supports canary and A/B rollouts with model variant routing and automatic fallback. We'll include a short how-to.
[06:04] [10:00 - NOTE: middle of meeting compressed in transcript]
[10:02] Daniel: Results from yesterday's shorter run — p95 for chat path at batch=1 was about 240ms; batch=4 pushed that to ~310ms; batch=8 to ~380ms. Throughput scaled roughly linearly to batch up to 8.
[10:22] Maya: Those p95 numbers mean batch=4 might be borderline. Can we try batch=3?
[10:26] Daniel: We can, but runtime batch sizes are typically powers or convenient sizes; we'll run 3 as a special. Expect intermediate results.
[10:34] Priya: For fallback and cost modeling, can you show a worst case where we regularly hit fallback to hosted?
[10:40] Ava: Yes — we'll simulate saturation with our stress run. We'll provide cost delta if 10% of requests go fallback. Historically that added ~12–20% to total spend depending on model choices.
[10:52] Omar: Any thoughts on scheduling — timeline wise, we want to decide pilot next steps by end of month. Does that align?
[10:58] Ava: Yes. If we run the benchmark this week and share results, we can have a pricing/commit proposal by 2026-12-22.
[11:07] Maya: One last operational question: can we purge KV entries or set TTLs? Some prompts are PII-sensitive.
[11:12] Daniel: Yes, cache TTL configurable and we can exclude certain prefixes from caching. KV is RAM-only and not logged by default; audit logs can be toggled.
[11:22] Priya: Sounds good, reiterate next concrete steps?
[11:26] Ava: Sure — redwood runs the extended benchmark (Daniel), share updated benchmark sheet (Ava), Lacuna shares prompt set and traffic distribution (Maya/Omar). We'll also send SOC2 and architecture doc.
[11:38] Maya: Great, thanks. That helps us pick between dedicated vs private.
[11:42] Ava: Cool — any random blockers?
[11:45] Omar: Need to confirm budget holder to sign reserved capacity if we go dedicated. I'll loop in finance after we see the numbers.
[11:52] Ava: Perfect. We'll aim to get things over in the next 48–72 hours. Thanks everyone.
[11:58] Priya: Thanks all.
[12:00] Meeting end.
